# Education in Poland
Children in Poland typically begin primary school (szkoła podstawowa) at age six or seven. Since 2017, primary education has been extended to eight years (grades 1–8), replacing the previous system of six years of primary school followed by three years of gimnazjum (junior high school), which was phased out by 2019. Upper secondary education starts after compulsory schooling and includes general secondary schools (liceum) lasting four years and various vocational and technical schools, such as five-year technical schools (technikum) leading to the Matura exam—a qualification for higher education—and three-year basic vocational schools granting vocational certificates. Special schools cater to mentally or physically handicapped students.
Poland’s tertiary education aligns with the Bologna process, typically offering three-year bachelor's degrees followed by two-year master's degrees; some long-cycle master’s programs last four to six years. Doctoral studies usually take about three years. Vocational education continues post-secondary through specialized schools lasting around two and a half years. University grading uses a numeric scale from 2.0 (fail) to 5.0 (highest), with half-point increments. Foreign language education is common, with English being the most studied, followed by German, French, Spanish, and Russian. The Polish educational system has a historical tradition of early emphasis on literacy and formal education, including one of the oldest universities in Europe—the Jagiellonian University founded in 1364. Recent reforms have modified the structure and curriculum with some criticism regarding nationalist and Eurocentric content in history education.
